Hi all,

I just discover  the https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/36120... Sorry if I reopen a point already discussed.

Before reviewing in details i have few questions, 

If  I have  well understood the PR there  is a single instance of a generic `IPC_service`.
Associated with this service only one backend is registered which is multi-instance
Then the `ipc_ept_cfg` struct is used to indentify the instance at application level.

Regarding possibility of backend, i can identify several types:
- RPMsg backend
- VIRTIO backends ( VIRTIO-I2C, VIRTIO- SCMI, ...)
- other standard or proprietary protocol

Using a single IPC_service instance, it seems that we can't support multiple backend types.
For example, how to handle an RPMsg backend and a Virtio backend in parallel?

Based on this  wouldn't it be more reliable  to manage the multi instance at `IPC_service` level?
And then declare each single backend instance using DT as proposed by @carlocaione ?

Then concerning the `ipc_rpmsg_multi_core` vs the `pc_rpmsg_multi-instance`. Is it a possibility to  merge both? 
Look to me that they are quite similar...

Thanks
Arnaud

Perhaps we could go by steps, renaming your backend  `ipc_rpmsg_backend.c` as it seems to integrated `ipc_rpmsg_multi-instance` constraintes. Then in a second step the `ipc_rpmsg_multi-instance` demo could be reworked to use your backend and finally clean the `ipc_rpmsg_multi-instance`

I propose a more gradual approach:
1. Rewrite the current `multi_instance` backend merging into it the `ipc_rpmsg_multi_instance` code, remove the `rpmsg_multi_instance` demo / code and separate the RPMsg handling into a separate "library". This is done because currently we only have hardware to test this backend.
2. Rewrite the content of this PR (`multi_core` backend) to support the new RPMsg "library".
3. Merge the two `multi_core` and `multi_instance` backends into one single backend.
4. Modify the IPC service code to support multiple backends at the same time.
5. (optional) Add the `rsc_table` backend.

By a separate "library", do you mean to move parts of code from `subsys/ipc/rpmsg_multi_instance/rpmsg_multi_instance.c` to a new library like `subsys/ipc/rpmsg_handling/` that could be used by various ipc_service backends?

Do you plan to replace the 'register_instance'  by 'ipc_service_register_backend(&backend, &inst)'  (in your 'multi-core' PR)?
This could avoid to manage the multi instance in the backend, as already handled by the support of the "multiple backends" in IPC service...

As far as the approach is concerned, I don't have a strong opinion. But look to me that the result goes in the right direction.

Thanks !
Arnaud

> Do you plan to replace the 'register_instance' by 'ipc_service_register_backend(&backend, &inst)' (in your 'multi-core' PR)?
> This could avoid to manage the multi instance in the backend, as already handled by the support of the "multiple backends" in IPC service...

Honestly? I have no idea right now how to manage multiple backends at the same time. But I was aiming at something easier, for example: 
1. Each backend is taking care of managing all the multiple instances of the same kind (i.e. all the instances with `compatible = <foobar>` are managed by the `foobar_backend.c`).
2. Each backend is still registering to the IPC service using the `ipc_service_register_backend()` call and the IPC service is taking care of (maybe) adding all the backend to some list
3. When an endpoint must be registered on a given instance, the IPC service is probing each registered backend to see if the instance is present in that backend.

I was not actually planning to have a general way to process multiple-instances that can be reused by multiple backends. This is mostly because each backend can have its own definition of "instance". So how a backend manages multiple instances is left to the backend itself.

> Are you sure you aren't actually creating a new driver API here?
...
>  this sure "smells" like a new device API

Yes, @mbolivar  I know that feeling :smile: (and I'm still pretty much conflicted about this).

There was a pretty long discussion with @hubertmis and @carlescufi about whether this should be a subsystem or a new device driver API. The conclusion was that given that the IPC / OpenAMP is not actually describing any real hardware (but it is only using other peripherals like shared memory, IPMs, etc...) it's probably better to have it as subsystem instead of a new device driver class (any other reason I'm missing @carlescufi ?)

But yeah, all the "ingredients" for a new device API are all there: compatibles, struct with hooks, different backends, etc...

At this point I'd like to summon @galak, because since I have to rework this I don't want to spend time on something that can be possibly NAK-ed on day 1 because it should have been a device API instead of a subsystem or viceversa.

I believe the confusion and the smell is caused by a new territory we enter with this PR.

So far devicetree was used to describe hardware and provide input to instantiate device drivers. This PR uses devicetree to describe system configuration. Based on this new description a generic subsystem (independent from hardware details, using generic driver APIs) is created.

 It looks Zephyr does not contain infrastructure to instantiate generic subsystems based on devicetree system configuration description yet, what causes the smell.

> It looks Zephyr does not contain infrastructure to instantiate generic subsystems based on devicetree system configuration description yet, what causes the smell.

I am not sure I agree with this. We have subsys/random and drivers/entropy as a counterexample, no?

> At this point I'd like to summon @galak, because since I have to rework this I don't want to spend time on something that can be possibly NAK-ed on day 1 because it should have been a device API instead of a subsystem or viceversa.

I added the dev-review tag so we can get some discussion on this this Thursday

> We have subsys/random and drivers/entropy as a counterexample, no?

I've reviewed subsys/random, but I can't find any entries in devicetree describing how to configure this subsystem (such as compatible="zephyr,random"). I understand the random subsystem is relatively simple and it does not require system configuration description in devicetree. If Zephyr supported multiple subsys/random instances running in parallel, each of them taking entropy from another source, it could make sense to describe these instances in the devicetree file.

I believe that's the main difference between subsys/random and subsys/ipc_service. The random subsystem in a single instance using a single driver (the one that is enabled). The ipc_service is controlling multiple OpenAMP instances, each of them using other set of ipm drivers, other shared memory region, and potentially targeting other CPU cluster. We would like to describe configuration of these instances using generic devicetree nodes (like compatible="ipc,rpmsg-mc").

issue_context.title: Add multi-core IPC service
issue_context.body:
With #36120 now merged we can start discussing how to extend the IPC service to support multi-core (>2) IPC.

The idea is that  the IPC Service backend implementation should be able to create several RPMsg instances based on DT information for IPC (shared memory regions, target CPU, IPM instances and mechanism, etc.. ) during system initialization. The API should allow the user to use any of the instances created without worrying about hardware details but only defining `target_cpu` and `endpoint_name`.

Tagging the relevant people: @maje-emb @hubertmis @carlescufi
comments:
I believe we would need to start with defining devicetree bindings describing IPC instances targeted to connect defined CPUs in the system. Based on such bindings we could create proper type in IPC Service API to define `target_cpu`.

I don't know if there are any works towards such devicetree bindings.

The main challenge I see is that devicetree entry for CPU A describing connection to CPU B would need to be a mirror of devicetree entry for CPU B describing connection to CPU A. It should be somehow handled by the scripts to ensure these entries are really mirrors.

> The main challenge I see is that devicetree entry for CPU A describing connection to CPU B would need to be a mirror of devicetree entry for CPU B describing connection to CPU A. It should be somehow handled by the scripts to ensure these entries are really mirrors.

@mbolivar-nordic @galak ^^

> The main challenge I see is that devicetree entry for CPU A describing connection to CPU B would need to be a mirror of devicetree entry for CPU B describing connection to CPU A. It should be somehow handled by the scripts to ensure these entries are really mirrors.

I don't think we should take the burden of verifying this. As it's the user job to be sure to use the correct regions in the DT, it should be the user job to ensure that the shared memory region between two cores are allocated correctly and matching among different DT.

I like both proposals how to extend DT.

I would rename `compatible = "ipc_multi_instance";` to something not implying software architecture (one could implement a software IPC service which can connect to multiple cores in single instance). `ipc_multi_core` or `ipc_multi_target` would be OK.

Also, I'm missing in both proposals information to which core given IPC is targeted. Let's imagine we have a system with Application CPU, Radio CPU, and DSP. Engineer crating Application CPU DT should create entries describing IPCs with both Radio and DSP. Engineer creating software for App CPU should not read DT to get information which entry is targeted to Radio and which to DSP. I think it should be clearly stated in DT in a way software can retrieve it. Is the label (`ipc_core12`, `core2`) the information that should identify target CPU for given IPC entry? Or should we add something more?

> Is the label (`ipc_core12`, `core2`) the information that should identify target CPU for given IPC entry? Or should we add something more?

Yes, I think we should add a new property for that, something like `target-name = <...>` so that we can use that to target the destination core.

I agree with your reasoning. With one exception:

> we could have multiple RPMsg instances between the same two cores but I don't see how that could be useful and the current driver doesn't support that

I understood the point of @maje-emb's patch was exactly to support multiple RPMsg instances between single pair of cores. Each instance uses separated memory region and separated IPM. The reasoning was to assign different priority to each instance. Abstract priority value can be translated to hardware IRQ priority level of IPM handler, or to software task priority level of the thread processing given instance. I don't know if there is any real use-case to create multiple RPMsg instances with different priorities between two cores. From my point of view, we can simplify IPC solution assuming there is single RPMsg instance per single pair of cores.

> @mbolivar-nordic @galak ^^

I didn't review the discussion in detail, but that seems to be one of the things that system devicetree is trying to solve. Absent a big change like that, I'm not sure we can enforce this with existing tooling any more than we can enforce consistent flash partition layouts between application and bootloader.
Some work about this going on at #37361

review_comments: Name of this macro gets a little confusing when we start adding system configuration alongside hardware description to devicetree. I think it could be renamed to `DT_NODE_COMPAT`, or an alias could be created. But it's out of scope of this patch.
I agree it is odd to see DT_DRV_COMPAT being used in subsys/ instead of drivers/. That's a code smell for sure, though maybe there's a good reason for it; I'm just digging into this.

Adding a new API that looks things up by string names feels a bit weird in "modern" Zephyr, by which I mean post-v2.5 Zephyr. We have everything we need to go from devicetree nodes to real devices, and this sure "smells" like a new device API, but I'm new to this area and so this is just intuition talking.
I think number of endpoint could be added to devicetree node as a new property, to allow variable number of endpoints between instances.

This too is "interesting-looking".

Are you sure you aren't actually creating a new driver API here?
Probably should be `ipc_rpmsg_multi_core`, or is it intentionally reusing `multi_instance` logger?
There might be multiple instances to single target. Should we add more arguments here to precisely select one?
Altenatively, we could prevent creating multiple instances for single target for now.
